utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Unfortunately, Judge Orie's not with us this morning because of urgent personal business. Therefore, the Trial Chamber will sit pursuant to Rule 15 bis. I guess we are supposed to carry on with the cross-examination of the witness. May the witness please be called into the courtroom. And while he comes in, just one little preliminary matter to raise with the witness who is supposed to come, Mr. Dean Manning. Five of the ten associated exhibits are very lengthy. The documents should be discussed in court and not be admitted as associated exhibits, and these documents are the following documents: Document with Rule 65 ter 04586, and that's 65 ter 05764, 65 ter 27979, 65 ter 27980, and 65 ter 27981.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's understood, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Groome. Good morning, Mr. Parsons.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning. Just to apologise for doing some other business as you were coming into the courtroom. Mr. Parsons, just to remind you that you are still bound by the declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Professor.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Reading yesterday's transcript with your testimony, I wanted only, before we begin, to clear up certain dilemmas that I have. Would you please tell the Court from whom did you in 2007 receive accreditation for your laboratories in which you do DNA matching?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The acronym for the German accreditation agency is D -- at that time was DACHS, which is the Deutsche Akkreditierungsstelle. That same organisation now has undergone some type of an internal name change, at least as far as the acronym goes. As far as I know it is DAkkS now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm asking you this because while running some checks of my own, I received information that the organisation under the acronym DAkkS, this German accreditation bureau, was established in 2009. Is this information correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That sounds like when they changed their name, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your assistance. Let me finish with this question. Did I understand you correctly when you said that from GEDNAP you never received any accreditation because they do not issue certificates for the work of laboratories?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certificates and accreditation aren't necessarily the same thing. As far as I know, GEDNAP is not an accreditation body; however, when one participates in their proficiency testing, one receives a letter concerning the outcome which might be considered a certificate, and we have received those.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you receive this letter from GEDNAP in 2007?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just let me clear up one more thing. In the official structure of the ICMP, is it on record that within their framework there is also the Podrinje Identification Project under the acronym PIP?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Presently, no, but in the past prior to formal transfer of the management of the PIP, yes, it would have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer. Could you also state for the record when did this formal hand-over or transition of the PIP take place?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, but I don't recall that date. I would say probably late 2010 or in 2011. I'm -- I really apologise for not being up on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now call up P1716. That is the summary report for the secondary grave site Cancari 04. And we need page 3, both in B/C/S and in English. Thank you. We now see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like a few clarifications on this subject very briefly and then we will deal with this substance of the summary. At one point we see alleged site origin, and against that line we see Kozluk, and one of the next lines is estimate number of bodies, we read 189. It is explained in greater detail in the text. Could you just tell us briefly, who is it exactly in the ICMP system who stands behind the alleged site origin?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure what you are saying -- what you are asking, Mr. Stojanovic. Who in the ICMP stands behind the alleged site origin, what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, Your Honour, bearing in mind the signatures on this document that the witness identified during examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But what do you mean by "stands behind"?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who is the person in the ICMP system who identifies the alleged site origin, where did they get that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Parsons, are you able to answer that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that I can be of assistance. First of all, this is an excavation site summary of the circumstances, observations, and conduct of activity with regard to the excavation of that site. As I mentioned yesterday, the ICMP does not work in a vacuum. This site was opened for excavation under court order, and has been identified as a mass grave through a great deal of investigatory information; and that information would be known to the ICMP forensic excavation team that was participating in this case and I don't recall the details. The type of evidence that has been involved in linking secondary graves to their primary graves has to do with shared items, such as recovery of the same type of ligatures, recovery of the same type of blindfolds, soil analysis, other artefacts such as an abundance of glass that is shared in both the primary and the secondary grave. Again, I don't recall the details of this particular site. And so when they in their summary report listed alleged site origin, they -- first of all, I will emphasise the word "alleged," meaning the understanding at the time of the excavation based on the type of evidence I referred to earlier and conducted by any number of agents such as the ICTY teams and/or -- I'm just looking to see under whose authority that this was excavated, I'm not seeing it right here, but the court order, et cetera. There's information indicating where this grave is considered to have arisen from. Certainly the archaeologists are very capable of ascertaining that it is a secondary rather than a primary grave, meaning that it has been moved or the contents have been moved from a different place and that's something that they can determine a priori from their investigations. And then lastly, you raised the general issue of linkage of sites. One of the predominant methods that we know one grave is linked to another is that we recover different parts of the same individual from one grave and the other despite the fact that they are very distantly geographically located.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Could you tell us, did any one of the three persons who signed this summary report - and I can will remind you, it's you, Andreas Kleiser and Sharna Daley. Can you stand by this conclusion on the alleged grave-site -- alleged site origin, that is, or is that information received from somebody else?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can stand -- all three of those people can stand behind the fact that that is the alleged site origin, but moreover, ICMP would be able to stand behind the connection on the basis of rigorous DNA linkage between that site and the Kozluk site. That information is actually not part of the excavation report, but nevertheless is additional confirmatory evidence that, in fact, demonstrates that that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is there anywhere, any evidence that connects a body in the primary grave in Kozluk and another part of the same body in the secondary grave-site Cancari 04?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, yes, but I'm not going to stand by that rigidly because we have many, many DNA to DNA linkages between primary and secondary grave-sites and I am almost positive that that reflects these -- the linkage of these two graves, but I'm sorry, I just don't have that memorised. We have that information that could be provided to the Court. I don't know if there will be other testimony later on that presents that type of summary information. We do have very definitive linkages between primary and secondary graves and I believe that this is among those.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will conclude with this. When we have such explicit and clear evidence, would it be necessary to include that type of information in this report?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think so. This is an excavation report, not a summary report of all findings with regard to subsequent DNA testing. Again, it simply lists the alleged site information here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand that the reasons for linkage are described in paragraph 39 of your summary report related to glass fragments, but now you've given a different answer. And we will try to find it if you tell us where, where could we find information about the linkage or the evidence that permits the linking from the primary grave Kozluk and the secondary grave Cancari 04?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could request it of the ICMP. I don't have the many thousands of linkages in my mind, but we have that DNA data clearly tabulated. There may be other investigators who have had access to our DNA information that could present evidence in that regard as well. That information can be clearly detected, in fact, from the match lists that have been provided and discussed yesterday where both the identification of the individual and the site location is listed. We could look at that at any time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will certainly check that officially and look further. Could you look back again at this page. It says "estimate number of bodies" in the secondary grave, 189. I don't want to take up any more time, but at page 14 in B/C/S and English page 9, in paragraph 35, we read that this estimate number was calculated based on an entire right pelvic bone. Who is the person who identified this estimate number of bodies and stated that this number will be defined prior to the autopsy and the examination of bodies in the morgue?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm going to start by simply reading paragraph 35. "Preliminary anthropological observations suggest that the remains were predominantly male and included young and older individuals. Some identifiable traits were observed during actual recovery of remains. From the archaeological record," and I insert my own words here now, meaning from the observations involved in this excavation, "the minimum number of individuals (MNI) has been calculated from the complete right femur and gives a number of 189 individuals. This figure is tentative pending final autopsy and examination in the mortuary." I think that reading that is self-explanatory with regard to the question that you asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That's precisely what I pointed out, but could you tell us by name who keeps these archaeological records and draws the conclusion that it is a minimal number of 189?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be the individuals involved in the field team and that information is kept by the ICMP.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I want to ask you this: The facts that we just discussed that indicate a linkage between the primary and secondary grave, do they permit the conclusion that all these bodies or parts of bodies are not necessarily from one primary grave, such as Kozluk?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you don't mind, please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps I wasn't clear enough. I'll put to you this: We believe that even if we get information that some of the bodies in the primary grave are identical in terms of DNA profile to bodies found in Cancari 04, it doesn't necessarily mean that all of 189 bodies or parts of bodies at Cancari 04 come from the primary grave Kozluk. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The establishment of that linkage is not exclusive. It is possible that bodies came from somewhere else as well, or body parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to look at P1717. That's a summary report on secondary grave-site Cancarski Put 08. Page 2 in B/C/S and page 2 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, in one of these lines here, it is stated that in the secondary grave Cancari Road 08, the estimated number of bodies is 84 based on the left tibia. If this is within your area of expertise, I want to ask you: Does this methodological approach here based on the left tibia correspond to the approach that you had in the Cancari Road -- in the Cancari 04 case, that is, the right femur underlying the estimate of the number of individuals?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Essentially yes. Let me explain how this minimum number of individuals is arrived at, and it's really quite a straightforward concept. So every person has exactly one right femur or one left tibia. We have a grave that consists of mixed body parts, and you want to know what is the minimum number of people that could be represented in that grave via at least one body part. So what you do is look for the unique body part, by that I mean the skeletal element of which an individual has only one of, look for the one that is the most frequent in that grave. So if there are ten right femurs, you know there are at least ten people represented in there. If in that same grave there are 15 left tibia, then that tibia and the femur could be from the same people, but you know that there are at least 15 people in that grave. There could be more. The emphasis here is on the minimum number of individuals. So it's always based on the most frequently represented unique element in the grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If you recall, following my learned friend Mr. Vanderpuye's showing of the document you discussed the link between the primary and this secondary grave, the primary grave being the Branjevo Farm in terms of the ligatures concerned. Can we comment on it briefly. In total, according to the reports shown to you by Mr. Vanderpuye, there were a number of ligatures and ropes that were found, the exact figure being 13. Do you recall it being shown to you yesterday during examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall seeing such a list. I don't recall any of the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could we briefly see the document in the B/C/S, it's page 16, and in the English -- I'm not sure at this point, but I believe we'll be able to find it. So page 16.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. If Mr. Stojanovic is looking for the list itself, it's page 16 in this exhibit, page 23 in the B/C/S, but I'm not sure if that's what he's looking for precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, Your Honour. Page 16 in the English, I think, and 24 in the B/C/S version. Thank you, Mr. Vanderpuye. The next page in the B/C/S, whereas the English page seems to be the right one. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Professor, in this annex of your report we have a list of 13 cases with description with documented ligatures and pieces of rope used for binding as you can see in front of you. These were found in the secondary grave. Why am I asking you this? According to the report, the estimated number of bodies found in the secondary grave is 84, the grave being Cancari 08, 13 ligatures were found corresponding to the artefacts extracted from the Branjevo primary grave. Would it be correct to draw the conclusion that it could not be established that all 84 bodies from the secondary grave Cancari 08 originate from the primary grave at Branjevo Farm?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'll start my answer by clarifying that it is not established that 84 bodies were found in Cancari grave 08, only that 84 -- based on this report, only that 84 I believe it was left tibia were found. So we don't necessarily have complete bodies. But to get to the main point of your question, it is true that based on the information that you've outlined here that we cannot -- that we do not conclude that they are all necessarily from Branjevo Farm.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask to be allowed to look at document number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me -- before you call the next document, Mr. Stojanovic. I'm trying to understand the underlying logic of your question. Is the underlying logic that because 84 bodies are claimed to have been found and only 13 ligatures, therefore are you then saying that all the people who were found at Branjevo Farm were bound in ligatures? Therefore, if we don't -- if we only find 13 ligatures, those who were not bound don't come from Branjevo Farm? Is that what we are supposed to understand from that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. We still believe that basically all of the people who perished in Branjevo were not bound by ligatures. You know that only the people on the first bus arrived bound. I can explain publicly why we are pursuing this line of questioning, with your leave. It is our position that we cannot arrive at a conclusion on the basis of that that all of the bodies originate from Branjevo and that the location where they had perished is not the place of execution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, that was precisely my question. So that is your underlying logic. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Of course you may, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, it is indeed under seal. Thank you for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So, Professor, I'll resume. "In very rare instances, the individual named on the DNA match report may not be consistent with the mortal remains from which the listed sample was taken. There are a number of reasons why this could be the case, such as the following: (1) there are additional relatives of the victim (such as a sibling) that are missing, but have not been reported to the ICMP (this can result in a named match report being issued for the wrong sibling) ..." My question is this: Is this the case you discussed yesterday during examination-in-chief by my learned friend Mr. Vanderpuye as an example from the chart where you mention it as the fact that the body of one of the missing siblings, one of the missing brothers, was identified?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your question as it came through in the translation is confusing and I'm not quite sure what point you're referring to with regard to the direct examination yesterday by Mr. Vanderpuye that you would like me to comment on. I would also like an opportunity before answering directly any questions to read the entire letter here to clearly understand the context and content.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. With the Court's permission --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before the witness reads the entire letter, can you re-state your question in a manner that is not confusing to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I will try to put my question in a different way, Professor. The ICMP representative says that these exceptions and potential mistakes in the course of the work done could be caused by the fact that there are relatives of the victim who are recorded as missing while not reported to the ICMP. How can this cause problems in the course of your work?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand that question and I will now read the letter in its entirety. I can proceed with a response now. And it does relate to some of the comments that were made yesterday with regard to DNA identification of the siblings, and we had stated that if, for example, the reference samples are parents, we can determine that a particular sample from one of their offspring is, indeed, related to those parents as an offspring; but if there are multiple children of those parents of the same sex, we are not able to distinguish among them by DNA alone. So if in the course of obtaining reports of missing persons there are two brothers missing but, for whatever reason, only one is reported to the ICMP, as far as we know there is only one missing offspring, only one missing child of these parents, his name is such and such. We find an offspring of those parents as represented in human remains, and we conclude that his name ought to be the person who's reported missing to us. If, however, not unknown to us - let me clarify that because it will come out as a double negative - if, however, unknown to us there is an additional sibling missing, it is possible that we would have the incorrect name on the match report. I would like to address your word "mistake." I wouldn't see that as a mistake. In other words, no error was committed in the testing process, but that's simply one of the uncertainties associated with such work in this context.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. In item 2 it reads: "There was mislabelling of the original sample cut for DNA, and the DNA match report is correct with regard to the individual who is the source of the sample, but the sample does not correspond to the correct case (this level is often outside of the control of the ICMP) ..." Could you make it clear for us what sort of potential mistakes does this address?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I would like to begin my answer in the context of this exhibit letter where the initial sentences emphasise that the ICMP considers the DNA match reports while in and of themselves extremely indicative of identity, that as essentially a quality-control measure prior to final identification of a body, that all evidence should be taken into account. And one of the issues that is controlled for in that process is that it is conceivable in any human activity for human error to mislabel or misdocument where a sample came from. So if there are, say, two bodies under investigation in the mortuary and a DNA sample is taken from one of them and it is mistakenly recorded that that DNA sample comes from a different body, a different case, it's submitted to the DNA laboratory, we will find out who the sample is really from by DNA if we make a match. And when we report that back, we will say sample labelled such and such comes from a particular individual. In the mortuary, under this unusual hypothetical example I'm giving you, they will then go open the case that corresponds to the label of the sample and see that it is inconsistent with the name of the individual. Let's say the named individual is 60 years old but the case in question is clearly by anthropological information 18 years old. They'll conclude that there has been some sort of a problem. And in this case the problem was that the original sample was mislabelled so they're not opening the correct body-bag where that case is stored. And in this way, a small number of cases that were represented in some of those other columns in the match list were detected.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I will conclude with this document with item 3 where another possibility of switch of samples is identified. Next we have three names referred to in the cases where it happened specifically. Save for the three names, are you aware of any other situations during the DNA matching process and identification?

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: By "situations" in the translation here, do you mean circumstances that can affect the matching process and identification?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely, Professor.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you would like me then to clarify the third point that we raised in our letter, that again refers to the inevitable possibility of human error and that relates to sample switches within the ICMP DNA laboratory. This is quite analogous to the mislabelling that I referred to that can take place outside of the ICMP. But within the ICMP if, for example, a tube containing the DNA of a particular individual is mislabelled as another individual, just simply has the wrong number on it, then again we would be mixing up which case is associated with that particular DNA identification. And again, there is no way to avoid the occurrence of human error absolutely in our work or in the work of any other forensic laboratory; however, particularly -- scratch the "particularly." However, we have in the case of our DNA laboratory system a very dynamic quality management system that continually monitors the opportunities for such errors to occur and attempts to systematically address those in preventative measures. So, for example, one place where it is comparatively likely to make a sample switch in the laboratory is where you're transferring the sample from one tube to another tube. And -- wait, wait, I'm not done. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]
utterances.text: And so we have implemented steps whereby independent witnesses check the order of the tubes before and after transfer. So, as we call it, an independent witness check to confirm as best as possible that things have been transferred correctly. So that's just a description of how we try to avoid those kind of instances, but I will tell you that we have in the laboratory detected a small number - I can't remember what number it is, it's probably below 20 - where those types of errors have been detected in the numerous thousands of cases that we've done. We look for them very, very closely and we correct them when they come to our attention. This letter relates to a particular instance apparently, I won't say the name, where one of these three possible sources of error apparently was -- apparently occurred and was subsequently detected by the ICMP and corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I seek to tender the 65 ter document 25220 under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No reaction from Mr. Vanderpuye. Yes, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 25220 receives number D327, Your Honours, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then it's admitted into evidence as D327, under seal. Mr. Stojanovic, I thought you had 45 minutes for today. How far are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one question, Your Honour, and out of an abundance of caution could that be done in private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Registrar. Dr. Parsons, we're going to take a break of 20 minutes. We'll come back to five to 11.00. Or maybe let's just find out before we go to a break. Do you have any re-examination at all, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I actually do, Mr. President, but it should be very brief, just maybe a handful of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which will take about five minutes or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So we'll come back after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll go for a break. You may follow the usher, Mr. Parsons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll take a break and come back at five to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please be brought into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I just have a few questions. If I could have, please, P1716 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE

utterances.speaker: THOMAS PARSONS [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thanks very much for that clarification, Dr. Parsons. I have no further questions for you. Thank you very much.
