utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, with your leave, I'd now like to read a short summary of this witness's evidence, the purpose of which I have explained to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may do so, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: In 1998, Dean Manning joined the Office of the Prosecutor of the ICTY and was assigned as a team investigator in the Srebrenica investigation. He subsequently became the co-ordinator of the Srebrenica exhumation programme. The programme included several objectives: To locate and exhume mass graves, determine if those graves were related to Srebrenica, determine the number of bodies in each of these graves, and attempt to identify, among other things, the individuals, their gender, cause of death, and injuries sustained. As co-ordinator, Mr. Manning worked closely with investigators, archaeologists, anthropologists, forensic pathologists, and several other professionals. He was responsible for the monitoring of the ICTY exhumations and for incorporating the results of those exhumations into the team's investigative work. ICTY investigations [sic] were carried out between 1996 and 2001. In 2001, the remaining graves were handed over to the Bosnian Commission for Missing Persons, the BCMP, which was assisted by the International Commission for Missing Persons, the ICMP. Any additional graves after this time were subsequently located by the BCMP. Manning personally visited some of these sites and reviewed the work of the Bosnian Commission's photographs and records. Manning and the Srebrenica investigation team identified the locations of the graves using aerial imagery of disturbed soil and witness accounts. After examining the data collected from the aerial imagery of mass graves, Mr. Manning was able to construct a time-frame in which each of these mass graves was created. Mr. Manning also discusses the forensic links between the primary and the secondary mass graves. Mr. Manning prepared three reports in 2000, 2001, and 2003, that summarised the evidence obtained from the exhumations from 1996 to 2001. Subsequently, in November 1997, Mr. Manning produced an updated report -- forgive me, November 2007 rather than November 1997 was the latter report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Manning produced -- this updated report specifically provided the number of individuals positively identified by DNA analysis in Srebrenica-related mass graves. Mr. Manning's work in updating this forensic evidence was subsequently taken over by Mr. Dusan Janc. And that concludes the summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Jeremy, if you have any questions, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I do have some additional questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, could you please state your current profession.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm a member of the Australian Federal Police and I'm currently the senior police liaison officer for the Middle East and I'm based in Dubai. I've held that position for the last three and a half years.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: In your prior testimony, you state that one of your primary duties as co-ordinator of the Srebrenica exhumation team was to function as a liaison with the Srebrenica autopsy and exhumations project that was occurring in Bosnia. Can you give a brief overview of the purpose of that exhumations and autopsy project.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, the exhumations during 1996 to 2000 were predominantly linked to the Srebrenica investigation. The purpose of the investigation was to locate, examine, exhume mass graves connected to the fall of Srebrenica, to examine the artefacts and exhibits within those graves, and to conduct autopsies of the human remains found with a view to identifying the individuals as persons but also to link them to the fall of Srebrenica and to the manner of their death and ultimately who was responsible for those offences.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And can you give an idea of the scale of this project?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: There were in excess of 40 mass graves, both primary and secondary, and to exhume a single mass grave would take many weeks, so generally a month or two, and in the field would involve between 20 and 30 people at the mass grave site, majority of which were experts, anthropologists and archaeologists, surveyors, forensic archaeological surveyors, police, crime scene officers and photographers, as well as logistic staff. At the mortuary in the town of Visoko, near Sarajevo, there was a similar team of about 20 individuals, mostly anthropologists, pathologists, forensic dentists, police scene of crime officers, and logistics staff. Generally it would be a several-million-dollar project each year and would involve a significant amount of effort which would go for the majority of the year, and ultimately, the experts examining those two phases would produce reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Can you give an idea of the sort of volume of paperwork that was generated by this project that -- perhaps the number of artefacts that were identified?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Because you're examining a very large mass grave in the middle of a remote location in Bosnia, everything was examined and photographed and video recorded. The artefacts, such as shell cases or blindfolds and ligatures, were treated as exhibits. We maintained a chain of continuity. We made records of where the bodies were found, we logged their positions, and when those bodies were conveyed to the mortuary there was a similar examination of the body and artefacts. Each autopsy report would generally run to ten pages. We would have tens of thousands of pages of autopsy reports. Throughout the programme there was at least 65.000 colour photographs taken of the exhumation and autopsy process. Each artefact would be examined and records would be created. So there was a very significant volume of documentation and photographs produced.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And focusing on your role within this project, how would you distinguish the role that you played in the field from the roles of other participants in the project?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was also an investigator with the team, so I also undertook interviews and witness statements and, where necessary, other duties. But primarily, I was a link between the investigation and the exhumation autopsy process. We had a process which went on over several years and involved a rotation, if you like, of experts. I was cast to look at the process and project from day one to day end and try and link all that material, all that evidence, and the expert reports and the documentation across that whole project and also to link what was happening in the field at the exhumations or the autopsies with our investigation. I also assisted the experts in -- not in preparing their reports, they did that independently, but assisting them in access to records, documentation, in some cases I would take the experts into the field. And following the creation of their expert reports, I examined those reports, provided them additional information if required, and then summarised a significant number of reports from experts.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And you mention in your previous written evidence three reports dated 2000, 2001, and 2003. The summaries -- the expert summaries you just referred to, are they included in those reports?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And do those reports also contain different, separate information relating to your personal, individual involvement in the exhumation project?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, they do, Your Honours. I examined the reports and the underlying data, the autopsy reports and the photographs, which had formed the basis of the reports made by the experts. But because, for instance, the chief archaeologist may have only been in the field for one season, he would not have seen in depth the previous material or the material that came after him. So I was examining all the material across the board. And, for instance, the exhumation project may say that -- not indicate there was a blindfold on a body. So the report from that expert would say that he hadn't seen a blindfold. The reason for that was because of the condition of the body. On arrival at Visoko mortuary, it would be examined and cleaned and they would see that there was clearly a blindfold on the body. So his report, the first report, would not indicate that blindfold, the second report would. In that instance, I examined every single report that went through the mortuary including every single blindfold and ligature, physically examined each of them, and examined the records behind those artefacts. Could I prove that that blindfold was indeed on the body? Was it photographed on the body? Where is the photograph? Was it included in an autopsy report? Was that autopsy report reflecting a blindfold? Was there a physical blindfold that matched that report? And the same for identifications, I would examine artefacts which had been recovered from the grave and either return them to The Hague for examination or return them to the Bosnian Commission for examination in an attempt to identify the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: You mention in your written evidence that a decision was taken in 2001 to hand-over responsibility for the un-exhumed graves to the Bosnian Commission for Missing Persons. Was the focus of that at the BCMP the same or different to the focus of the ICTY exhumation team?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: The focus was different. The ICTY project was predominantly a forensic examination to provide evidence to this Court. It was considered vital that the evidence be preserved, that we examined how the graves were made, how the individuals came to be in the graves, and how they were killed. The Bosnian Commission - who were monitored by ICMP and the ICMP officers were present at the exhumations - their goal was to recover the bodies and I think I'm correct in saying as quickly as possible with a view to identifying the bodies. Their role was to open the graves, if possible examine the evidence, but predominantly remove the bodies, take them to the mortuary, and have them identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And in your written evidence you state that, in 2005, you began to review the work of the Bosnian authorities and the ICMP and you prepared a report in November 2007 in respect to that review. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, could the Court Officer please bring 65 ter 05764 to our screens. This should be Mr. Manning's November 2007 report.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, the report's now on the screen before you. Is that the report that you produced in November 2007?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And can you briefly describe the process that you went through in reviewing the work of the BCMP, also include some details about the ICMP's role in that work.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Effectively, I was asked to examine the results of the DNA analysis connected to Srebrenica. I went to Bosnia, visited ICMP facilities, and the Bosnian Commission for Missing Persons, as well as the Tuzla canton court. And what I did was examine the process of how the DNA was recovered, how the process was conducted, how the reassociation of bodies was conducted. But predominantly I was there to seek the data, the positive DNA identifications for Srebrenica. Eventually I was given access to that data. I looked at positive identifications or identifications of individuals who were unique individuals not yet identified. And I took that data and produced a table which showed the graves that the ICTY were aware of and how many individuals had been identified in those graves via DNA analysis. I didn't include the names, but I included the body reference from our exhumations and the DNA result from ICMP. And that provided a definitive count of individuals, unique individuals, located within the graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And you explain in your written evidence in the Popovic transcript that in this table that you refer to there were -- an error was made, a basic numerical error. Now, that's described in your written evidence and I don't propose to take you back through that again, but could you confirm that that's correct?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: That's correct, and I noted that error and produced a document to that error. As a result, not only did I examine the report but other staff members from OTP examined the report to seek any other errors and I don't believe there are any other errors. And that error was a mistake on my part.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please go to page -- e-court page 27 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Manning, this is the first of a series of pages of data that actually run until the end of this document from page 27 onwards. Can you explain what this information is, please?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, these are the data that I obtained from ICMP. If you look in the case ID column, there is a case which is CSK, for instance, 38. That's from the Cerska grave, primary mass grave, and it indicates that a body known as CSK-38 has been identified by ICMP. The second and third column contains an identification number produced by ICMP. A, it indicates that there is a unique DNA profile for Cerska 38 and that there is a case ID for the identification of that individual. And if you like, Cerska 38 has been identified as a unique individual based on a DNA analysis from his remains or her remains and a sample provided by family members.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And was your work in reviewing this DNA information taken over by another former ICTY investigator?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Do you recall the name of that investigator?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Dusan Janc. He was an investigator with the Srebrenica team.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you mention a mass grave, you mention the Cerska primary mass grave. Can you explain what you mean by a mass grave, both primary mass grave and secondary mass graves which you refer to in your written evidence?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, the archaeologist would have a strict definition of a mass grave, but for the Srebrenica investigation it was effectively a grave that contained multiple human remains. We could say, you know, two people is a mass grave, but generally we were dealing with graves which were very large, and a mass grave is a grave that contains the remains of at least two people and multiple human remains. In the case of, say, Glogova or Kozluk mass graves, many hundreds of individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, may I just interrupt a little bit and I apologise if you've explained this before. What is a unique individual?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the mass graves which were disturbed, that is, they've been opened up and bodies removed, meant that the individuals in the grave were broken up. So if you have an undisturbed grave where the bodies are placed, you open the grave and you have ten individuals. In our graves, the majority were disturbed. So you had individuals broken apart, part of them in one grave, part in another, and indeed part in a third. That meant that you would have what you thought represented most of a body in one grave and part of -- most of what represented a body in a second grave. With the DNA analysis, they would say: We've checked the remains and the DNA profile which is -- and I'm not a DNA expert, but the DNA profile is unique to that individual. So they would then take three parts of a body and bring them together. Well, even though there were three separate parts, they were a unique individual, they represented one DNA sample.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, you've referred to mass graves and you've explained what those are. Could you also explain what you consider to be a primary mass grave and a secondary mass grave?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: A primary mass grave is effectively the grave in which the bodies are placed at the time of or immediately after death. In the case of many of the Srebrenica sites, they were actually executed at the grave-site. So they're buried in a primary mass grave, and if that grave is not disturbed, we could then open the grave and see the bodies as they were placed in the grave or as they died. In this instance, several months after the bodies were buried in July of 1995, there was an operation to open many of the primary graves, and they opened up those graves and they removed individuals from the grave, I believe with the intention of removing all the individuals which they did not do. They would then take those human remains from the primary grave, transport them to a secondary grave, that is, a grave that has been dug since the primary grave, put them in the primary [sic] grave and seal that grave up. You then had a primary disturbed grave which had -- either had most of the bodies removed or a significant part and those bodies were transported to a secondary grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, could we please see on our screens Exhibit MFI P01481. And this is a book of aerial imagery of primary and secondary mass graves. I'd like to go to page 7 of that book, please. And, Your Honours, I do have this chart in a hard copy A3 size if that would be of assistance to you. We will be using it a little bit in the direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It would be indeed useful, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic has a copy and with his permission it might be helpful to provide it to the witness as well, with your permission as well, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic -- no objection, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, do you recognise the document before you?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I produced this document for a previous court appearance.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And can you explain the document?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document was designed to provide an overview of where the mass graves were, both primary and secondary, but most importantly to show the movement of bodies from primary disturbed graves to secondary graves. It also indicates execution points in black. The red is primary mass graves. The green dots are secondary mass graves. And it also shows the area -- that the graves were confined to an area from Pilica Dom in the north to Zeleni Jadar in the south, which was the zone of responsibility of the Drina Corps as I understand it. And I produced the map to also show why we associated primary to secondary. And if you see within the rectangles the reasons why we, at that stage, link the primary and secondary mass graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we please see another document on our screens, 65 ter 04610. This is an image of the body from the Kozluk mass grave. And can we rotate that to the left, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, do you recognise this image?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And in the context of what you've been saying about the primary and the secondary mass graves, can you explain what we see in this particular photo?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This is a photo of the Kozluk mass grave which was adjacent to the Drina River. It was a primary mass grave and execution point. If you see there are skeletonised remains of the victims on the middle and top of the image, and you can see from the posture of many of them that their hands are bound. Effectively, these men and boys were shot at that site and they were shot and killed where they lay. Then the soil was placed on top of that mass of bodies, so they were effectively covered up and buried. When the archaeologist removed the soil, you saw the bodies laying on the surface of the ground and that surface was the surface as it was in 1995. And if you - and I've seen this in mass graves where I've been present where I've stood within the graves - you can see to the bottom right-hand side a large part of that original surface and some of the bodies is missing. You can see to the far middle right teeth marks in the soil, and what that clearly shows, even to me as a non-archaeological expert, is that a machine has come in and taken away that chunk of soil. You can see that it's taken away some of the bodies and it's cut through the original surface on which the bodies lay. So what you have is evidence of someone coming in after the bodies were placed on the ground, after they were covered up, and taking out that section of the grave and, if you like, that section of the grave was then taken to a secondary mass grave. And that missing part would form part of the secondary mass grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You mentioned teeth marks. You say: "You can see to the far middle right teeth marks in the soil ..." You're obviously not talking about teeth marks of a human being, you're talking about maybe a pay loader or something like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'm sorry. In this case, you can see that a machine was used to dig that out and the teeth marks I refer to are the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are the machine's teeth marks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, are the blades. And you can actually see the teeth of the digging machine carving into the soil. And in this image, when it's a bit lighter you can clearly see those teeth marks through the wall of the soil.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, just to be clear, the trench that you -- that you've described that we see in the bottom right corner, that wasn't created by the ICTY exhumation team?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: No. They very, very carefully removed the top layer of soil, the overburden, with the intention of showing what the grave looked like, and you can see they've done a very effective job with the mass of bodies. And imagine that soil has now been painstakingly lifted off and as they did -- and I have seen this happen, as they did they say, well, this cut here was filled with soil. We've removed the soil and you can see the cut edges of that. So they didn't create that. The robbers, the people who removed the bodies created that trench. They simply revealed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I'd like to tender that image, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That image is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you not able to switch on your microphone?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No, I am, Your Honour, thank you. Document 04610 receives number P1731, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, I'd now like to discuss aerial imagery which you make reference to in your written evidence. Can you briefly explain how the exhumations team and how you in particular made use of this aerial imagery?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, aerial imagery was provided to the OTP which was effectively images of areas of disturbed soil. Initially they were released by Madeleine Albright from the US government, and they showed clearly disturbances. In one image of Nova Kasaba, they showed four areas of disturbance which was ultimately examined and shown to be a primary undisturbed mass grave. We would use those images in an attempt to identify mass graves. We would go to the area depicted. For instance, I would hold the image, I would look at the ground with the archaeologists. For instance, at Zeleni Jadar 06, we stood on the roadway depicted in the image, we looked at the image and we said: Well, where is the mass grave? We think it's here. The image is distorted somewhat. We think it's there. We would then identify the area, demine the area, scrape off the soil, and discover the outline of a mass grave. It would then be trenched to confirm it was a mass grave. So they were -- they allowed us to search through the country-side for suspected mass grave sites and exhume them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And did any of the mass grave sites that you identified on the basis of this aerial imagery, were they marked or identified in any particular way, and I'm thinking with tombstones or ...?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: No, none of them were. And, in fact, the majority, if not all, of the mass graves were in very remote areas, particularly the secondary mass graves. They were in areas where the entire population had been removed, all the homes had been destroyed, and they were in quite remote locations. And there was no indication, by way of a sign or a post of any other indication, that these were mass grave sites. In fact, the majority of them were difficult to find even though we had the imagery showing us where we thought they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, could we please see on our screens again P01481, MFI. That's the aerial imagery book.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, are you familiar with this book of aerial images?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And in the course of your investigations, were you able to discern any sort of pattern, any discernible pattern relating to the creation of the primary and secondary mass graves?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, the images initially would show the creation date of the primary mass graves, which was in July of 1995. Unfortunately, the -- unfortunately, sometimes it would be a window, so they would say on the 5th of July until the 17th of July was the available imagery. And you would see on the 5th of July no mass grave was created, and then at the end of that window you would see a mass grave created. When they were disturbing and robbing the primary mass graves, which was in September and October of 1995, at the same time they were opening up the secondary mass graves. These mass graves did not exist prior to the primary graves being opened up again. They would open up the primary graves, transport the bodies to the secondary grave, close the primary grave, and close the secondary grave. In effect, those secondary graves were created as a direct result of the disturbance of the primary graves as a place to place the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we go to page 17 in e-court of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, could you tell us, if you're able, what we're looking at here.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a split image and that's that window of available images. So on the left-hand pane is an area -- what we refer to Orahovac or Lipje. So on the 5th of July, 1995, you can see some ruined houses and some roadways and the thick white line is the railway line. On the 27th of July, 1995, you can clearly see two areas of heavily disturbed soil, which is the Lipje or Orahovac 1 and 2 primary mass graves. One is at the middle bottom of the screen over the railway line and one is at the top middle of the screen, top right of the screen, between those two small roads, and that's a primary mass grave which I was present for the opening of that grave and most of the exhumation of that grave and also the examination or re-examination of the other mass grave, Orahovac 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: You mention the grave was known as Orahovac 1 and 2 or Lipje --

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Sorry --

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I see on the charts that Lipje's in a different location?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I think it was Lazete, LZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Can we go to the next page in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, if you could again tell us what we're looking at here, please.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Again, a split screen. The one on the left is the 7th of September, and the one on the right, the 27th of September. So the primary mass grave of LZ-01 is shown on the left-hand pane and you can see that it's been overgrown and it hasn't been disturbed again from the previous image, but you can see on the 27th of September or up to the 27th of September there's been a significant disturbance of that site. And on a better-quality image you can see motor vehicle tracks and what is clearly the blades of a heavy machine moving the soil around on that mass grave site. And I indicate that the yellow lettering at the bottom which indicates Lazete 01 and Lazete 01, both sides, was placed there by myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And the white lettering that we see, did you place that there, the date --

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yeah, the black lettering in the white boxes was placed by the provider of the imagery.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Can we go to the next page, please, page 19.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And, again, Mr. Manning, can you explain what we're looking at here?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Again a split image, exactly the same time-frame, and this is the next grave across the railway line which you can see in the top left and right of the image. Again, you see the very large area of disturbance on the left which is then strongly disturbed on the right pane. So between the 7th of September and the 27th of September, that mass grave was opened up and the majority of the bodies were removed. And again, clearly you can see vehicle tracks on that -- particularly on the right-hand image.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we go to page 44 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, could you tell us what we're looking at here.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This is a series of images which are produced with the OTP which are three separate aerial images stitched together, and they show the section of road which we called Hodzici road and they show a series of seven secondary mass graves, starting at Hodzici 1, and these graves are circled and again the letters were placed there by myself. And they show the secondary mass graves which by various means were linked to the Orahovac second -- primary mass grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And could we go to page 49 of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And again, once we get there, Mr. Manning, if you could explain what we're looking at, please.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: This is the before photo, if you like. So on the 7th of September, 1995, you can see a road forking and ruined houses, and in that area along the Hodzici road there were no people. All the homes were destroyed and all the population had left. So it was quite remote. And you can see -- and the image is not so clear, but there is no area of disturbance on that image.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And can we go to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And if you could explain what we're looking at here.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Okay, you can see the fork in the road, and what wasn't there in the previous image is now two secondary mass graves, Hodzici 5 on the left and Hodzici 4 on the right. Those mass graves were created, filled with bodies, and in this image closed up and covered up. And they would bulldoze or move the earth across a grave and completely level the soil so that you would be looking at not a pile of dirt or a partial hole, but a levelled field which had been disturbed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would be moving on to a different topic now. I wonder if it might be the right time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed it will be. We take a break and come back at about quarter past 12.00. Mr. Manning, you may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We take a break and come back at quarter past 12.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, in the previous session we were discussing your November 2007 report and in relation to the DNA analysis, and you were -- you were asked a question about what a unique individual actually was. Now, I'd like to clarify with you, is there a distinction between a unique individual who has been identified by name and a unique individual who has not been identified by name?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, in terms of my 2007 report, there is, but effectively the DNA simply means that that DNA is unique to a single individual. And that -- I use that term particularly because of the way the bodies are broken up. But in my report, the ICMP would identify from the DNA profile a missing person from Srebrenica. So therefore, that would be an ID of a unique individual who now has a name. In that report there was also a number of individuals who presented as a unique DNA profile in that -- that that profile wasn't represented by any other remains. And -- but that person had not yet been identified. So you had someone who was definitely an individual, a collection of bones perhaps from different graves, who was definitely one person but they did not yet know who that person or what that person's name was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Okay. You mentioned earlier today shell casings and I'd like to show you an exhibit, 65 ter 05154.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: If that could be brought to our screens, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, do you -- do you recognise the image on the screen before us; and if so, are you able to comment upon what we see?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, I recognise the image. It's an individual at the Kozluk primary mass grave, and I think it's a body 501 which would be KK-501 or a similar number. You can see from that image a number of things. One is there's a blindfold on the individual's face covering their eyes. You can see part of that cloth on the back of the head. You can see their arms are behind their back and I know that that individual is bound. So that person is blindfolded and is bound. But what else you can see in that image, in the colour version you can see a significant amount of green glass, broken green glass bottles. And if you look in the top left-hand middle corner you can see a round shape which is a bottle cap. And that green glass was from a dumping-ground from a bottling factory and that was all over the Kozluk site. And in the bottom middle of the image you can see a shell case, a 7.62-millimetre shell case, and that's laying near the body's arm. So you have a shell case next to the body, you have the broken green glass around the body, you have the body bound and blindfolded, and executed at that site in Kozluk.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, we've -- to step away from this image for a moment, we discussed satellite imagery of -- or aerial imagery of mass graves this morning. We have hard copies of those aerial images which I'd like to provide to you, and we also have two volumes of the photos of the blindfolds and ligatures also in hard copy. We'd like to make those available to the Chamber. The Defence have copies of those which I provided this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And we have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Ivetic. That's fine, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And the 65 ter numbers of those, the blindfolds books volume 1 and 2, 65 ter numbers 27979 and 27980, and the aerial imagery book is 27981.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you tendering these books, as you've given these 65 ter numbers, or are you just telling us what they are?

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I'm not tendering those right now. I will tender them at the conclusion of the direct examination, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, were all of the shell casings that you have referred to and the shell casings you identified in your investigations, were all of those shell casings collected?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: We didn't collect all the shell cases within a mass grave. We took not a representative sample, but we took a number of shell cases. There were often so many that you couldn't collect them all, simply a logistical issue, also some were damaged. But the ones that we collected, particularly those associated with a body or the surface of the grave were collected by us, examined, and ultimately sent to the US Alcohol, Tobacco, and Firearms service for examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I'd like to tender that image on the screen before us, 65 ter 05154.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Madam Registrar, the image is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 05154 receives number P1732, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, you mentioned that shell casings were transferred to the US Alcohol, Tobacco, and Firearms service for examination. What examination was requested by the OTP, by your team?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Effectively it was in two parts, but part one was to examine the shell cases that we'd collected and to examine the markings on the shell cases predominantly caused by the ejection of the shell from the weapon, and see if we could match shell cases from not only within the grave but across the primary and secondary graves, and effectively show if a group of weapons were present at the exhumation -- executions. So it was an examination of the shell cases to find matches.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could the Court Officer please bring 65 ter 25728 to our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: While this is coming up, Mr. Manning, it's an OTP information report relating to shell casings that you have just discussed, in particular the analysis by the ATF. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I do, yes. It effectively matches the results ATF examination of the shell cases to our grave locations. And if you see an ERN reference and then a location, it effectively says the ATF provided reference numbers for the shell cases which matched, and we can see in this that the shell case from Kozluk matched a shell case from Cancari Road grave 03, a secondary grave. And it's effectively matching shell cases found in primary graves to those found in secondary graves or within areas of the grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And are those matches pictorially represented on the image that we have before us, the -- the chart of the primary and secondary mass graves, the A3 hard copy?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I added where there were matching shell cases to this diagram, and if you look, for instance, from Kozluk, you'll see that it was matched by bottle labels and the green glass I spoke of and also shell cases. So a shell case from the Kozluk primary grave matched a shell case from the Cancari Road secondary graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender that exhibit, 65 ter 25728.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Registrar -- it's admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 25728 receives number P1733, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could the Court Officer please bring up 65 ter 04586, and this is Mr. Manning's June 2000 report. And I'd like to go to page 16, please, e-court page 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, do you recognise this chart on the screen before you?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I produced it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And what does this show?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, it shows the previous data, but rather more simply in that a shell case from Kravica warehouse was matched to a shell case from Zeleni Jadar 5 secondary grave and it goes to show matches between primary and secondary graves. In the case of Cerska, it shows a shell case within the mass grave which had been covered up, matched shell cases found on the surface, but more importantly on the roadway and on the north side of the road in Cerska, which provided to us corroboration that the individuals were shot at that site and that the shell cases found on the roadway and the road were from the weapon or weapons that killed those individuals. And some of those shell cases then found their way into the grave with the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And you referred to the connection between a shell casing from Kravica warehouse to the Zeleni Jadar 5 grave. Looking at the A3 image that we have of primary and secondary graves, I don't see a connection between Kravica warehouse and Zeleni Jadar. Can you explain why that isn't pictorially represented?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Kravica warehouse is an execution point where a significant number of men and boys were killed. We have very strong evidence that those bodies were then transported to three primary mass graves, that is, Ravnice which we refer to as Ravnice 1 and 2, and Glogova 1 and 2. The shell case that was found in Zeleni Jadar 5, and Zeleni Jadar 5 is linked to Glogova 1 and 2, had to have come to that secondary grave via the primary grave. At the time the warehouse execution took place, Zeleni Jadar 5 had not been created. So I could not show the movement of the bodies, in this case indicated by the shell case, direct from the warehouse to Zeleni Jadar 5 because the route was from the warehouse to Glogova 1 and 2, which was then disturbed and the bodies were taken to a very remote location at Zeleni Jadar and placed in the secondary grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And looking at this table from your 2000 report which is on the screen before us, I see on the top of the page it states: "The examination provided that shell casings located at the following areas were fired by the same weapon; that is, that the weapon was either at each of the sites or the shell casings were transported from one site to the other." Can you explain how as part of your investigation you interpreted those expert results?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Well, initially the report from the ATF had detailed numbers that were not our numbers, so I had to match up the reference numbers from the ATF to our reference numbers, and hence that previous document which showed the links. And what, certainly to me, that means is if the weapon at Kravica which was fired and a shell case ejected at Kravica, that individual weapon was then fired at Zeleni Jadar 5 some several months later or, as is indicated by the other evidence, the shell case was transported with the bodies from the execution point to the primary mass grave and then to the secondary mass grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And did your investigations indicate that there were any suggestions that the same weapon was present at each of those sites?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: If I understand correctly, no, because, as I say, Zeleni Jadar, for instance, wasn't a battle scene, it wasn't created when the original executions happened. So there's no indication that the weapon was taken and fired at two different locations. Multiplied by all the primary and secondary graves, it's clear from the evidence that the people were executed and placed in primary graves and the related shell cases are taken in the removal process and placed in the secondary graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I'd like to now discuss the blindfolds and ligatures you've made reference to.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Your Honours, could we please see 65 ter 15203 [Realtime transcript read in error "15023"] on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, do you recognise this document; and if so, can you tell us what it relates to?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, I produced that table or both tables, and it shows the ligatures and blindfolds which were located in the Srebrenica mass graves. I indicated before that a part of the process might not be able to identify a blindfold or a ligature, and I was tasked with finding out how many blindfolds and ligatures we actually had. So what I did was I went to the mortuary and I examined every blindfold and every ligature physically, and then I traced the continuity of every single blindfold and ligature. So if there was a reference in an autopsy report to a blindfold, I took that report, I looked for photos which substantiated that, and you saw in the previous image a blindfold on a body. Then I took the autopsy report, looked for the photographic logs, looked for the examination by the crime scene officers, looked for the examination by the pathologist. And if I was satisfied that we had a continuous chain of evidence indicating a blindfold was either found on a body or with a body and that it had the characteristics of a blindfold or a ligature, and if I could prove that process, then I accepted that as a blindfold or a ligature. If I couldn't, if there was a break in that chain, or if the photograph hadn't been taken or I couldn't prove that chain, I rejected that item. And I produced this table, A, to show a total of the blindfolds and ligatures and where they were from; and B, where they were located. In the instance for ligatures, we see how many were on the wrists or arms. And, for instance, in Cerska the arms would come away from the body or the wrists and finger bones, phalanges, would come away, but you would still see a wire loop around the forearm of the individual, the bones. Some ligatures and some blindfolds were very closely associated with the bodies, that is, they had fallen off perhaps at the time of death or perhaps at the time of disturbance or, indeed, as we were exhuming the bodies, and I noted that, particularly where the blindfold or ligature was effectively on top of the body. And I also have a column for ligatures loose in the grave. This is where the ligature was very definitely removed by perhaps several centimetres or a metre from the body but was still very clearly a ligature. It had the shape of a figure eight if it was wire or cloth and it was clearly used to bind someone's hands. And if I could show those characteristics, I accepted it as a ligature, and I did the same thing for the blindfolds. And I was extraordinarily conservative in that count. I wanted to make sure that I could prove every single item across the entire time-frame of the exhumations process and show that they were blindfolds and ligatures.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go back to your 2007 report, please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy, just for the sake of the record, what was the correct 65 ter number of this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Because in the transcript we see another number, I think it's just a typo, page 55, line 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: And I'd like to tender that document now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 15203 receives number P1734, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Could we go to 04586, the 2007 report, please. And I'd like to go to e-court page 115.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: Mr. Manning, you mentioned ligatures identified in Cerska. Can you just very briefly tell us what we're looking at here, then we'll move to some photographs.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes. I produced this table to show the references to the ligatures from Cerska. The individuals at Cerska who were bound were bound by wire and mostly steel, strong steel wire, although with some electrical wire with black coating. It shows the ERN number of the item, the case number which would be the body, Cerska 6 in the case of the first one, and a description and location of the ligature.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: I'd like to now move to a different topic. On the basis of your investigation into the Srebrenica-related mass graves, both primary and secondary, did your investigations reveal any evidence that suggested that those mass graves contained combat-related casualties or bodies that were the product of combat or fighting? And if you can perhaps provide some general observations and if you have any specific observations related to the graves we see on the A3 chart before us, please provide those as well.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, part of the exhumation process and autopsy process was to identify how these individuals died, and we were very conscious of the fact that we needed to seek evidence of either the fact that they had been killed in an execution or they were the result of battle casualties. So that was in our mind in our examinations. The evidence that we have, particularly from the primary mass graves, is that individuals were not killed as a result of a battle. They weren't picked up and placed in sanitary mass graves. They were executed, and they were placed in mass graves in an attempt to hide the bodies. And remembering, if they were sanitary graves, they should be marked and they should allow after the conflict for those graves to be identified and the bodies removed or at least dealt with in a different manner. And to my view, the primary mass graves and certainly the secondary mass graves were hidden. They were placed in areas which were quite remote. But if you look at, for instance, Cerska which we were discussing the wire ligatures, there is 150, roughly, individuals in that primary, undisturbed mass grave and a significant number of those men are bound and they were shot at that location. There is evidence of them being shot in that location, falling by the side of the road, and being covered up. Not all the men were bound or there wasn't evidence that all the men were bound, but the ones that weren't bound were in the same condition, in the same process, as the ones that were bound. So I believe that the evidence shows that all those individuals were killed at the same time in the same manner because if they were picked up in the battle-field, you would see that reflected in the way that they were placed in the grave. And I'm not an archaeologist and I'm not an expert on soil or that process, but if you look at it, if you pick a body up with a machine, you will pick up a layer of soil and leaves and sand and dirt and whatever the body is laying on. And if you place that body in a pit or a grave, you will see that layer of soil and you will see several layers of bodies interspersed with several layers of soil. Or if they were thrown into the grave, you will see that in the posture of the bodies. So if they're physically picked up and carried and placed in a grave, you will see that. And what we saw in almost all the graves, particularly the primary graves, is that the individuals had a consistency about them. The Kozluk mass grave, we have evidence that they were placed and made to kneel amongst broken glass in a rubbish pit. Many of them were bound and blindfolded, and they were shot there and they tumbled forward and were covered up with soil. Now, not all the bodies were blindfolded or ligatured, but again there is that consistency, you see that image of the bodies laying on the surface of the ground and there's nothing to say, to show, that they were picked up in different locations. And at the execution point of Kravica warehouse, when those bodies were taken to the primary mass graves, they reflected that they were killed at the warehouse. There were pieces of the warehouse, there were pieces of machinery, there was straw, there was evidence that followed those bodies from the warehouse to the primary mass graves and to the secondary mass graves. And that -- and in Nova Kasaba, 96 bodies again were bound and shot in situ. And you have that consistency across the graves, and we were looking for indications that these individuals were killed in battle; and what we saw and what I believe to be the case is that they were held captive, executed, and buried.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: You mentioned locations, you mentioned that the graves you located were often in very isolated areas. Were those areas areas that were connected to the route of the column as revealed by your investigations, the route of the column of Muslims leaving Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Not at all. I don't believe that you can say that the mass graves were located and the execution points are located in areas of battle, except for Kravica warehouse which was clearly in the path of the column. But those men were taken prisoner and they were held and then executed. If you look at Kozluk, it's on the border with the Drina River. It's a completely isolated location. From memory, the Drina Wolves had a base a kilometre from the execution point and there was no evidence of a battle in that location. The dam at Petkovci, there was no battle there. Branjevo Military Farm is significantly removed from the areas of conflict, as is the Pilica Dom.
