utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, while we're waiting for the witness, can you give us an idea of your time estimation? I know there's been a bit of a change.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the time estimate for this witness is three and a half hours for cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Three and a half hours, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Down from six, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, did you at any time during the course of your employment with the Office of the Prosecutor have any role in either drafting, preparing, or revising any of the indictments against General Ratko Mladic?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I don't believe I did. I don't believe I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. And how about any of the indictments that were brought by the ICTY against others for the events in Srebrenica municipality in July of 1995, did you assist in or participate in the drafting or revising of any of those indictments during your tenure?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Well, I was part of the Srebrenica team for almost four years, so in that period I believe we amended indictments against a number of individuals, and I would have been part of that process as a member of the team. As team members, we would assist in that process and provide information or review material to make sure it was correct as far as we were aware. So, yes, I would have been part of that process. I can't remember specific instances.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: With the caveat that you can't remember specific instances, do you consider that you have a personal interest in seeing those indictments that you assisted in amending come to fruition with the conviction of persons under the same?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I came to -- I came to the Tribunal because I wish to see and be part of an investigation of war crimes, and across that time I've become involved in investigations directed to war crimes and seeing individuals brought to this and other courts in the building. So I had a -- an involvement and an interest in seeing those investigations carried to their conclusion, which is in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I understand as an investigator. I'm talking as a witness, sir, since you are also testifying as a witness. Do you think that you have or feel that you have a personal interest as a witness in seeing these indictments which you assisted in drafting or amending come to fruition with the conviction of persons under the same?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I don't think that's up to me. What I'm doing is presenting my evidence and my information and presenting what I know before the Court, and with the -- with the hope that the outcome will be based on what was presented to the Court. I don't think it's correct to say I have a personal interest outside of my employment or as a witness in this Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay, sir. I see from the CV that we still have up on the screen that one of the other investigations or cases you dealt with was the 1991 massacre of civilians at Ovcara. Did any of your work in that case also relate to exhumations or was it strictly standard investigation of facts or witnesses?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Again, in that instance I was the team leader, so I was co-ordinating their activities. Investigators had dealt with the Ovcara exhumation. It was the same team I had worked with and I visited the scene, but I wasn't actively involved in the on-the-ground investigations. I was co-ordinating the activities of the team of investigators and analysts.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, looking at the bottom half of the page that we have on the screen, from 1998 to 2002, some of the activities you were involved in included the establishment of working guide-lines and protocols with the Bosnian Commission as well as ICMP, other NGOs, and SFOR. Was this only in 2000 or did you have a role in the same type of activity for any time prior to 2000?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: That was specifically related to the hand-over of responsibility for the mass graves to the Bosnian Commission, and that related to that process.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you know if protocols or guide-lines existed for the work of these named organisations prior to the year 2000?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, I believe they had protocols. They had certainly processes in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, focusing on the Office of the Prosecutor and your work there, at any time while you were employed by them did there exist, first of all, any guide-lines or protocols dealing with the examination of potential witnesses or suspects in the interview process?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, there were a set of guide-lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And how about in relation to the investigations relating to exhumations? Now, I understand from your prior transcripts that have now been received into evidence, there was protocols for anthropologists, but I want to ask you about different protocols, specifically focusing on the work done by its -- by the Prosecution's own investigators working on exhumations. Were there any protocols or guide-lines for that work, sir?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: The work of the investigators was, to some degree, detailed by the archaeological and pathological guide-lines in that they would outline some activities the investigators would be involved in. But predominantly those guide-lines were on the exhumation autopsy process, and we did not have specific guide-lines as to how the Srebrenica team investigators would work with the exhumation autopsy teams that I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, in answering my question you have mentioned archaeological and pathological guide-lines. Were those promulgated or drafted by the Office of the Prosecutor or by someone else?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I'm referring specifically to the chief archaeologist, for instance, Mr. Richard Wright -- or Professor Richard Wright and also John Clark, the chief pathologist who had both had -- I think they refer to them in their expert reports, both had guide-lines for their operations and how their staff would conduct their activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Do you appreciate and would agree that proper procedures including chain of custody and care in exhumations and recovery of artefacts are important to preserve the evidence obtained from a site and safe-guard it from potential contamination or tampering?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you feel that the ICTY personnel working with you on the exhumations that you were involved in accomplished the goal of taking sufficient care to safe-guard and prevent tampering and contamination of items removed from the exhumation sites?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now if we could turn the page in both versions to the second page of this document in e-court, and just to follow-up on my promise of earlier, I think we can see at the bottom of the page -- well, we could for a second there, we could see at the bottom of the page that this was the 2003 CV.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to ask you about something you have here, it's the third bullet point from the top of the page in English, and it says here you: "Presented this report and other evidence in the trial of Senior Bosnian Serb General Krstic who was convicted and sentenced in August 2001 of Genocide and other war crimes." Sir, is this you in essence bragging about obtaining a conviction on a case that you testified in?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Was this one of the cases where you had assisted in drafting or revising the indictment?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, my involvement in the Krstic case was a part of a team. I did a great deal of work, but so did the rest of the team. I've indicated in this CV that I was involved in the case of General Krstic and that he was convicted as a result of the evidence presented to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I think that was the answer to my previous question, my question about is this perhaps one of the cases you assisted in drafting the indictment. Can you remember?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: No, I can't, and I suspect that the indictment was created prior to my joining the team. I think we may have amended the indictment and I may have had some involvement in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Let me ask you this: Back in Australia, would it be part of your work as an investigator or a police investigator to draft and prepare indictments against suspects or is that work handled by a separate prosecutor's office?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Australian model sees the director of public prosecutions separate to the police investigation; however, in drafting their indictments or their presentations to the court, we would have some input and we would be providing advice. But it's a much greater separation in Australia.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the fifth bullet point from the top in the English, you describe your work on witness and suspect interviews and you mention the test firing and examination of 2500 seized weapons and 5.000 shell casings. Now, today during your direct examination we heard some talk of shell casings, but I wanted to ask you about the weapons and I want to be very clear and make sure that we're understanding exactly everything that you did. First of all, am I correct that as part of the Office of the Prosecutor investigations you had occasion to seize a certain number of weapons from the VRS barracks of the Bratunac and Zvornik Brigades to test fire them so as to see if they could be linked to any of the bullet casings found at the various execution and burial sites?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: That's correct. I was part of the team that seized the weapons and I co-ordinated the test firing and the continuity of the shell cases obtained.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now if you could clarify for me. This CV mentions the amount of 2500. Was it 2500 weapons or a thousand weapons or -- that were part of the seizure and the test firing that we've talked about?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: We seized over several days a large number of weapons. Referring to this, I accept that it was 2500, 2.500 weapons, and that those weapons that could be fired we test fired and obtained shell cases, which we had ultimately tested.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I think the easiest way to do this is to go to 65 ter number 1D1113 in e-court to revisit some of the testimony from the Popovic proceedings. And if we can turn to page 20 of the same in e-court, that ought to correlate to transcript page 19094.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, you can follow along as I read into the record line 8 through 25. And then I'll have some follow-up questions for you based upon that. "Q. I would like to put to you the answer you gave in the Blagojevic case on page 7209. "I've been trying to find the documents from the batch from my learned friends concerning an analysis of around 1.000 rifles that we know was carried out, and I'm referring to the rifles that were taken from the barracks. "In answer to Mr. Karnavas' question, you said, Your Honours: "[In English] 'In a major part of that process, we tried to [indiscernible] from the Bratunac/Zvornik Brigade and other brigades or units in the area of Srebrenica. These weapons were test-fired and cases were collected with the intention of comparing. That was conducted by Mr. Ols and his associates. Did not recall the ultimate outcome, but I understand it was unsuccessful.' "A. Your Honours, I agree with that statement, and we are discussing the same matter. To my knowledge, the test firing produced many hundreds of shell cases. They were examined, and those results were negative. But I wasn't involved in that final part of the process, but I agree with you that they were negative." First of all, sir, do you stand by this prior testimony as being both truthful and accurate as to the matters contained therein, such that you would so testify today if asked these same questions?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now you'll see the reason for my confusion. Your CV mentions 2500 rifles, yet in Popovic there was talk of 1.000 rifles. Can you tell me which one is right or is -- are they both right, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Well, I'm not referring to a thousand rifles. I can't now recall the number, but it was very significant. If I recorded in my CV 2.500 in 2003, I accept that. We seized the weapons that we believed appropriate. Ultimately, we took them to a firing range. Some of them could not be fired; many could. We fired as many as we could. And I accept that there were would have been 2.500 weapons and we conducted a test firing process ultimately that was negative. No weapons were linked to shell cases from the mass graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if we could return to your CV, which is again 65 ter number 19388 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could return to page 2 of the same in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, working back -- backwards in time now, at the time when you were a detective-sergeant from 1997 to 1998, am I correct that during that time-period your police work in Australia dealt with internal matters and did not deal with investigation of any crimes committed by non-police?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Effectively my job was to investigate police officers, but it was somewhat wider in that I could investigate other government agencies. And if an allegation concerned, for instance, drug dealing, we would investigate the drug dealing and the officer alleged to be involved. So on occasion, we would investigate other people, but predominantly internal investigation -- serious internal investigations against police.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. During that time-period - again, we're discussing just 1997 through 1998 - did you have occasion to participate in any exhumations?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And moving, again, backwards in time, during 1994 through 1996 as a senior detective, did you at that time have to participate in any exhumations of suspected or actual graves?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I can say no and indicate that I -- prior to coming to the ICTY I was involved in one exhumation, which was a removal of a body from a customary grave to another grave. It wasn't a criminal investigation. I was there as an oversight from the legal point of view.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Did you have occasion to work with any archaeologists or anthropologists as to their work on mortal remains of suspected crime victims during the time-period that you were employed as a member of the Australian police force at any capacity?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now the same question as to pathologists or medical coroners. Did you have occasion to work with them at any time while you were a member of the Australian police?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: From about 1985 until I came to the Tribunal in 1998, I was involved in a significant number of investigations of sudden death and/or murder and suicide. I attended, if not a hundred, tens of autopsies, and that was part of my general duties and to deal with pathologists related to that examination, that investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn to the next page in both versions of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The last thing I want to ask you about on this document is the relevant training and education, and you have here listed ICTY internal induction and training courses. How long was this training?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I can't remember the initial training. I think it was only a week, but that was in 1998. And we also undertook some training during the following years, and I also was instructing on interview techniques and witness interviews later on in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did any of the training that you undertook at the ICTY deal with exhumation investigations?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Not in great depth, but I do recall some examination of the -- what I think would have perhaps been Orahovac and Cerska, but not in great depth, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And what about chain of custody protocols, were those covered in your induction training at the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: To my knowledge, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd seek to tender 65 ter number 19388 into evidence at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Jeremy.

utterances.speaker: MR. JEREMY
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document receives number D328, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. If we can call up the Popovic transcript again, that's 65 ter number 1D1112, and page 24 of the same in e-court, which should be underlying transcript page 19017.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, in relation to the questioning about your 2005 report, which has been marked for identification in this case, you were questioned as follows, and I will read -- and you can follow on from line 7 through to line 21. "Q. Will you agree with me, and I'm referring to the report, that the purpose of the two-week mission in Bosnia was to collect archaeological, anthropological, pathological, and other forensic -- I apologise -- archaeological, anthropological, pathological and other forensic data collected during the exhumations and autopsies after 2001. "A. That's correct. "Q. Thank you. In the biweekly period, you were supposed to process the data that had to do with several different scientific branches. You did spend some time with the experts there, but you are not qualified in any of the aforementioned sciences that would qualify you to conduct this task? "A. Your Honours, I would agree that I'm not qualified. I have no formal qualifications certainly in those disciplines. I believe I am qualified to have undertaken this task and to have travelled to Bosnia to gain that data, the information." Sir, do you stand by this prior testimony as being both truthful and accurate as to the matters contained therein?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And would you so testify again the same way if asked these same questions?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, I presume that when you came to the Prosecution in 1998, that you were handed over material information by your predecessors in investigations; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: The team provided briefing material, and I was briefed by the team leader and the team members, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You say "by the team leader and the team members," do you recall the names of any of these individuals?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: The team leader at the time was Jean Rene Ruez. I certainly received a briefing from him. The trial attorney involved in that case at the time was Mr. Peter McCloskey. I received a briefing from him and also I discussed the case, reviewed the material, and read material from the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Was one of the persons that briefed you Jan Kruszewski?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, in your reports authored in 2000, 2001, 2005, and also 2007 which summarise the findings of various experts in relation to various mass grave sites, you talk about several that are based on the work of a Dr. William Haglund. Did you have a chance to work with him or was he someone that predated you at the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, I didn't work on an exhumation with Dr. Haglund, but I did deal with him extensively in preparation for his reports and his appearances in court, and I also dealt with him in a process outside the Tribunal where he was part of a training team for war crimes investigations.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would you consider that the work of Dr. Haglund was central to the exhumations that had been performed by the Office of the Prosecutor in the years prior to your arrival to the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Dr. Haglund conducted the autopsy -- sorry, the exhumation and autopsy process in 1996 for Srebrenica, so yes. And in 1997 it was another team. In 1998, some exhumations were conducted prior to my arrival by Professor Wright, and thereafter I dealt with Professor Wright and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I know -- you and I both know which sites we're talking about. Let's make it clear for the Judges who might not know the material as well as we do. Am I correct that the -- when you say "related for Srebrenica," am I correct that Dr. Haglund performed the work on the graves at Cerska, the Nova Kasaba 1996 location, Orahovac 2, which is also called Lazete 2, and Branjevo Farm, which is also called Pilica?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in addition to working on Srebrenica-related graves, is it correct that Dr. Haglund also worked on graves in other parts of the Balkans, including relating to Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, I believe he was involved in Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in your reports there is an organisation identified Physicians for Human Rights or PHR for short. Can you tell me if I'm correct that they were a partner or co-sponsor alongside the Office of the Prosecutor for some of the exhumation and autopsy work that was conducted in the years prior to your arrival at the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I confirm that there was a joint team of ICTY and PHR that conducted the 1996 exhumations for Srebrenica. I'm not sure about 1997, but thereafter, at least for Srebrenica, it was -- PHR were an NGO we dealt with and not a partner.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you ever have occasion to work with personnel from PHR, Physicians for Human Rights, in the course of your duties as a member of the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, I did -- I sought information from PHR. They provided identification documentation. They provided access to the -- to some family members, and I dealt with PHR on and off for several years mainly based in their office in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to go over something with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's 65 ter number 1D1114 in e-court. And if we could focus on the first page and the top of that page for the moment. There we go. Now hopefully we can read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, the preamble of this document says that: "At the request of the United Nations International Criminal Tribunal and the Office of the Chief Prosecutor located in The Hague, Netherlands, a panel of forensic anthropologists and pathologists was convened at the office of the Bexar County Medical Examiner, San Antonio, Texas, from the 14th to the 19th of November, 1997." And then it lists the members of the panels and names some five forensic practitioners present and two absent. It also identifies both attorney Peter McCloskey and investigator Jan Kruszewski as being present. Now, you identified both Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Kruszewski as persons who briefed you when you came to the Tribunal. Were you briefed as part of your training and introduction to the Tribunal and your preparation for work --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please slow down. Please slow down, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, you have identified both of them as individuals who briefed you when you came to the Tribunal. Did either of them inform you of this panel that had met from the 14th to the 19th of November, 1997, in San Antonio, Texas?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can't remember a specific briefing. I was aware of the issue. In fact, I thought rather than Jan Kruszewski, it was Asif Syed who was involved with Mr. McCloskey, but I was aware generally that there were a number of allegations and that those allegations were investigated. And thereafter I had little or nothing to do with that process.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And when you say that you are aware of a number of allegations, would those be allegations relating to the work of the joint OTP/PHR exhumations teams in 1996 under the reins of Dr. Haglund and Dr. Kirschner?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I believe the allegations were in some respects personal in nature about Dr. Haglund and there were allegations that some autopsy reports had been altered and I understand that was fully investigated. And as I say, I didn't have any involvement in that process. I have been asked about that in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn to the second page of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you mentioned the name of Dr. Haglund and a second name, and that is, in my view, not properly recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Dr. Kirschner. And perhaps I should ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You and I both know about Dr. Kirschner. Are we talking about the same person, William Kirschner or Bill Kirschner.

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, I know Dr. Kirschner.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I believe that's K-i-r-s-c-h-n-e-r. And Dr. Kirschner was the pathologist working under Dr. Haglund; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, here under II on the document we have the specified task, and it talks about members of the teams that were interviewed and it lists a number of individuals. And there on the bottom of the screen we can see the name of Dr. Haglund and Dr. Kirschner. Do you recognise the names of the other persons listed here as persons who would have worked on ICTY exhumations predating your employment with the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion in the dealings with PHR personnel to deal with any of the persons who are listed here?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: In dealing with PHR, I don't believe so. No, I don't believe so. I mainly dealt with the director of PHR in Tuzla, whose name escapes me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's fair enough, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can go to the next page of this document in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At the bottom of the page, the part that says: "Even within their own country there are differences in investigation and autopsy techniques, interpretation of findings, and differences between professional disciplines, pathology, anthropology, criminal investigatory practices -- procedures, and evidence collection. There was also a potential, if not real, conflict between the UN and PHR personnel as well as variations on legal opinion for cause and manner of death. There was an attempt to use the Minnesota Protocol, a standardised form for the autopsy recording which was developed in the early 1980's." Now, sir, are you familiar with the Minnesota Protocol?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you know if the Minnesota Protocol was utilised in the exhumations work that you would have participated in that followed 1998 and onwards?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I don't believe so, not called the Minnesota Protocol.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: One more question before we take the break. How about the so-called Istanbul Protocol for preserving evidence as to torture or cruel and inhumane treatment? Was that forensic protocol employed successfully in the exhumations and investigations that you were involved in?

utterances.speaker: DEAN MANNING
utterances.text: I don't recall the protocol being referred to as the Istanbul Protocol, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're at the time for today's break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Manning, unfortunately we can't finish with you today. You'll have to come back tomorrow morning. Before you leave, just to warn you that you may not talk to anybody whosoever about the testimony you have given or still to give until you are formally excused from further testifying.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. You will come back here tomorrow morning at 9.00 in the morning, courtroom III -- 9.30, I'm sorry, Mr. Manning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 9.30 tomorrow morning, this courtroom, tomorrow, the 11th. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We stand adjourned to 11th of July, 2013, Courtroom III, 9.30 in the morning. Court adjourned.
